strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing underexplored gap between conventional embodied AI tasks and realistic personalized assistance scenarios requiring memory-grounded context understanding

Well-designed two-stage evaluation framework that cleverly isolates memory utilization effects by keeping scene and goal constant while varying instructions, with principled categorization into object semantics and user patterns

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families and scales (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Qwen, Llama) with extensive analysis including top-k memory ablations, error/success case taxonomy, and supplementary investigations of trajectory importance and ambiguous instructions

Clear and significant findings demonstrating concrete limitations: user patterns substantially harder than object semantics, irrelevant memories reliably degrade performance, smaller models struggle compoundingly with multi-memory tasks, consistent across model families
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation descriptions, prompts in appendix, dataset statistics, and careful documentation of dataset construction process
Effective presentation with clear figures (especially Figure 2) and well-organized writing that successfully communicates complex evaluation methodology
weaknesses: Critical real-world applicability limitations: oracle skills for perception/motor control and deliberate exclusion of visual perception fundamentally simplify the problem to high-level planning rather than full embodied task execution; simulation-only evaluation without real-world validation

Dataset quality concerns undermine benchmark reliability: only 438 episodes across 12 scenes is small scale; 13.4% filtering rate (31 episodes with zero success rate) raises questions about task design and introduces potential evaluation bias; heavy reliance on GPT-4o for data generation while simultaneously evaluating GPT-4o creates circularity

Artificial memory retrieval setup with guaranteed correct memory inclusion (randomly replacing if not initially retrieved) doesn't reflect realistic retrieval challenges and significantly weakens claims about memory utilization difficulties; no exploration of modern retrieval-augmented generation or memory enhancement methods

Limited technical novelty: framework contribution is primarily organizational rather than technically novel; findings (LLMs struggle with multi-step reasoning over complex sequences) are well-established and largely confirmatory rather than surprising

Insufficient depth of analysis: paper identifies problems but doesn't adequately explain mechanisms or propose solutions; limited investigation into why certain personalized knowledge is harder to utilize; supplementary findings (ambiguous instructions) are only proof-of-concept

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing on main results; no statistical comparison of model performance differences; dataset statistics and quality control process deserve more prominent documentation

Incomplete experimental coverage: no comparison with memory enhancement techniques or retrieval augmentation; no ablations on memory encoding or retrieval strategies; no baseline with simpler memory systems; generalization to other domains and scales unclear

Narrow scope limits impact: restricted to object rearrangement tasks with relatively simple personalized knowledge; unclear how framework scales to complex personalization scenarios, larger memory stores, or real-world messy episodic memory with failures and irrelevant events

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem addressing the gap between instruction-following and personalization in embodied agents
Elegant two-stage evaluation framework that effectively isolates memory's impact through careful experimental design
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models with thorough analysis including knowledge-type breakdowns, top-k analysis, and memory quality comparisons
Significant empirical findings clearly demonstrating substantial limitations even in frontier models (30.5% drop for GPT-4o on joint-memory tasks)
Valuable insights into failure modes with clear taxonomy of success/failure cases and qualitative analysis
Strong reproducibility with extensive implementation details, prompts, and dataset documentation
Thoughtful ethical considerations and societal impact discussion
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visualizations
weaknesses: Severely limited real-world applicability: experiments entirely in controlled simulator with oracle perception and motor skills, excluding VLMs/VLA models and realistic noise
Unrealistic memory retrieval setup: top-5 retrieval with guaranteed correct memory inclusion doesn't reflect real retrieval challenges
Relatively small dataset (438 episodes across 12 scenes) with heavy reliance on GPT-4o for generation and quality control, creating potential circularity
Primarily diagnostic paper without proposed solutions or methods to improve performance; discussion of alternatives (Section 6.1-6.2) is incomplete
Insufficient root cause analysis: doesn't clearly separate issues of retrieval accuracy, memory representation, and LLM reasoning capability
Limited methodological novelty: two-stage evaluation is sound but straightforward; knowledge categorization is intuitive but not novel
Missing comparisons with memory-augmented architectures, alternative retrieval methods, or prompt optimization strategies
Weak statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; small sample sizes per condition
Findings are somewhat expected (LLMs struggle with complex multi-step memory reasoning) without surprising insights
Scope limited to object rearrangement in residential settings; generalization to other embodied tasks unclear

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem addressing memory utilization in personalized embodied agents, an understudied area with clear practical relevance
MEMENTO evaluation framework is methodologically sound with clever two-stage design that isolates memory utilization by holding scenes/goals constant while varying instructions
Comprehensive experimental analysis across 6 models with systematic investigation of bottlenecks, particularly information overload (Figure 6) and coordination failures (Section 5.2)
Clear decomposition of personalized knowledge into object semantics and user patterns with well-defined subcategories, providing structured lens for analysis
Thorough dataset construction with inter-rater reliability validation (Krippendorff's α=0.69), quality control procedures, and manual review
Concrete error taxonomy (Figure 5) with detailed examples showing specific failure modes and successful patterns
Extensive supplementary materials including human baselines (E.1), memory quality analysis (E.2), robustness testing (E.2.2), and prompts for reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: simulation-only (Habitat 3.0, 12 scenes, 438 episodes), oracle perception and motor skills, single task type (object rearrangement). These simplifications critically limit generalizability to real embodied agents where vision and action are primary failure modes.

Artificial experimental setup: gold memory forced into top-k results removes realistic retrieval challenges. Figure 11 shows sharp degradation with retrieved vs. gold memory, suggesting findings may not transfer to realistic conditions with imperfect memory retrieval.

Shallow mechanistic analysis: paper identifies bottlenecks (information overload, commonsense vs. personalized knowledge preference, coordination failures) but doesn't explain *why* they occur or propose targeted solutions beyond the final user-profile memory module.
Limited technical novelty: user-profile memory applies established knowledge graph techniques without ablations on design choices or comparisons with alternative structured memory architectures.

Solution evaluation concerns: user-profile memory assumes perfect knowledge extraction; no analysis of errors from LLM-based graph construction (Algorithm 1) or retrieval reformulation (Algorithm 2). Modest improvements and absolute performance remains concerning.

Incomplete statistical analysis: no confidence intervals or significance testing despite small episode counts (201 acquisition); memory summarization tested on only 30 episodes; joint-memory baseline design (averaging two acquisition episodes) complicates comparison.

Narrow generalization: findings specific to object rearrangement in single simulation; unclear if results hold for other embodied tasks, realistic perception/action noise, or large-scale memory pools (1000s of interactions).

Conversational abilities gap: acknowledged but significant limitation—real personalized assistance requires clarification, proactive engagement, and communication adaptation beyond memory utilization.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation that clearly articulates the gap between conventional embodied tasks and practical personalized assistance requiring episodic memory
Thoughtfully designed MEMENTO evaluation framework that elegantly isolates memory utilization through a two-stage design with fixed environments/goals but varying instructions
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 diverse LLM models with rigorous dataset construction (438 episodes, inter-rater reliability analysis, quality filtering)
Clear and actionable findings identifying concrete bottlenecks: information overload with increased memory context and coordination failures on joint-memory tasks
Important insight that episodic memory provides both personalized knowledge AND in-context learning benefits, explaining why simple summarization fails for smaller models
Exceptional reproducibility and transparency: complete implementation details, all prompts, example trajectories, human baseline validation, promised code release
Strong solution validated across all model sizes showing substantial improvements, particularly on user patterns where agents struggled most
weaknesses: All evaluation conducted in Habitat 3.0 simulator with oracle perception/motor skills and guaranteed gold memories in retrieval top-k, limiting generalization to real robots and realistic retrieval scenarios
Synthetic data generated by GPT-4o with only moderate inter-rater reliability (α=0.69; some criteria as low as 0.57-0.58), and same model used for baseline testing creates potential circular bias
Limited baseline comparisons: no evaluation against other memory-augmented agent approaches (MemGPT, A-Mem) or simpler retrieval-augmented prompting strategies
Proposed hierarchical knowledge graph solution is somewhat incremental, combining standard knowledge graph representation with LLM reformulation; no comparison with alternative knowledge structures
Narrow task and domain scope restricted to object rearrangement in households; generalization to other embodied tasks (navigation, manipulation) and real environments unexplored
Root cause analysis is superficial regarding why agents struggle with sequential user patterns; limited exploration of prompt engineering or reasoning approaches to mitigate issues
Methodological concerns: binary success metric doesn't capture partial progress, no systematic statistical significance testing, small sample sizes for real-world scenarios (30-41 tasks)

Missing practical elements acknowledged but significant: no conversational clarification, no handling of evolving user preferences, no user studies validating relevance of retrieved memories, no cost analysis
